name: Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP)
description: CHIP gives low-cost health coverage to Texas children whose families earn too much for Medicaid but cannot afford private insurance. A child must be 18 or younger, live in Texas, be a U.S. citizen or qualified non-citizen, and be in a family within the income guidelines, which top out at 201% of the federal poverty level and apply once income is above the Children's Medicaid limit. A 90-day wait without other insurance applies unless a good-cause exemption is met. Coverage includes checkups, dental care, medicine, vaccines, hospital care, vision and hearing care, and specialists. Depending on income, families may pay an enrollment fee of $50 or less per year and small copays. Children with disabilities who earn too much may look at the Medicaid Buy-In for Children program. The monthly value shown is an estimate of government CHIP spending per Texas enrollee, not cash the household receives.
documents_needed: Proof of income (last two pay stubs or paychecks, employer statement, or self-employment records)
Proof of citizenship (U.S. passport, Certificate of Naturalization, U.S. birth certificate, hospital record of birth, or Medicare card)
Immigration status papers (resident card I-551, I-94, or USCIS papers), if applicable
Proof of identity (driver's license or Texas DPS ID)
Proof of Texas residence (utility bill, rent receipt, or landlord letter)
Unpaid medical bills or statements from the past three months

name: Children's Medicaid (STAR)
description: Children's Medicaid provides free health coverage for Texas children in low-income families. A child must be 18 or younger (some children with disabilities who are 19 or 20 can also qualify), live in Texas, be a U.S. citizen or qualified non-citizen, and be in a family within the income guidelines. Monthly income limits depend on the child's age: 198% of the federal poverty level for children under 1, 144% for ages 1 to 5, and 133% for ages 6 to 18. Coverage includes checkups, dental care, medicine, vaccines, hospital care, vision and hearing care, and specialists, plus long-term services for children with disabilities. If family income is too high, HHSC automatically checks whether the child can get CHIP instead. The monthly value shown is an estimate of government Medicaid spending per month for each Texas non-disabled child enrollee, from the HHSC Reference Guide chart (year not labeled), not cash the household receives.
documents_needed: Proof of income (last two pay stubs or paychecks, employer statement, or self-employment records)
Proof of citizenship (U.S. passport, Certificate of Naturalization, U.S. birth certificate, hospital record of birth, or Medicare card)
Immigration status papers (resident card I-551, I-94, or USCIS papers), if applicable
Proof of identity (driver's license or Texas DPS ID)
Proof of Texas residence (utility bill, rent receipt, or landlord letter)
Unpaid medical bills or statements from the past three months

name: Medicaid for Pregnant Women (STAR)
description: Medicaid for Pregnant Women gives free health coverage to low-income pregnant women in Texas during pregnancy and for up to 12 months after the baby is born. The applicant must live in Texas and be a U.S. citizen or qualified non-citizen, and family income must be at or below 198% of the federal poverty level, which was $2,634 a month for a family of one in the March 2026 table and rises with family size. It includes full Medicaid benefits such as prenatal visits and vitamins, labor and delivery, and checkups for the baby. HHSC must decide within 15 business days and does not require an interview. Women who do not qualify for Medicaid may qualify for CHIP Perinatal instead. The monthly value shown is an estimate of government Medicaid spending per Texas enrollee in MACPAC's "other adult" group (adults who qualify through pregnancy, or as parents and caretakers) in fiscal year 2023, divided by 12. No pregnancy-only figure is published. It is not cash the household receives.
documents_needed: Proof of income (two pay stubs or paychecks from the last 60 days, employer statement, or self-employment records)
Proof of citizenship (U.S. passport, Certificate of Naturalization, U.S. birth certificate, hospital record of birth, or Medicare card)
Immigration status papers (resident card I-551, I-94, or USCIS papers), if applicable
Proof of identity (driver's license or Texas DPS ID)
Proof of Texas residence (utility bill, rent receipt, or landlord letter)
Unpaid medical bills or statements from the past three months

name: CHIP Perinatal
description: CHIP Perinatal covers prenatal care for the unborn child of a pregnant Texas woman who cannot get Medicaid and has no other health insurance. A woman qualifies if her household income is between 199% and 202% of the federal poverty level, or is at or below 202% but she does not qualify for Medicaid because of immigration status. Women who are U.S. citizens or qualified immigrants at or below 198% may qualify for Medicaid instead. Coverage includes prenatal visits, medicine such as prenatal vitamins, labor and delivery, and two doctor visits after the pregnancy ends. The 90-day waiting period, enrollment fees and copays of regular CHIP do not apply. A woman must apply before the baby is born, and HHSC has 15 business days to process the application. The monthly value shown is an estimate based on general CHIP spending per Texas enrollee (no perinatal figure is published), not cash the household receives.
documents_needed: Proof of income (paycheck stub from the last 60 days, last year's tax return, self-employment proof, employer letter, or Social Security statement)
Proof of allowable expenses, if claimed (previous year's federal tax return; divorce decree or court order for alimony paid)

name: Emergency Medicaid
description: Emergency Medicaid pays for treatment of an emergency medical condition for Texans who would qualify for Medicaid except for their immigration status. It can cover pregnant women, children under 19, parents and caretaker relatives, and elderly or disabled adults who are non-immigrants, undocumented, or certain permanent residents who do not meet the alien status rules. Income limits follow the regular program: 198% of the federal poverty level for pregnant women and children under 1, 144% for ages 1 to 5, and 133% for ages 6 to 18; elderly or disabled adults must meet SSI rules other than citizenship. Only services needed to stabilize the emergency are covered, and the treating practitioner must certify it on Form H3038. Children get 12 months of coverage and pregnant women coverage through 12 months after delivery.
documents_needed: Form H3038, Emergency Medical Services Certification, signed by the treating practitioner
Proof of identity (driver's license or Texas DPS ID)
Proof of income (pay stubs, employer statement, or self-employment records)
Proof of Texas residence (utility bill, rent receipt, or landlord letter)

name: Medicaid for the Elderly and People with Disabilities (MEPD)
description: MEPD gives health coverage, and in many cases long-term care, to Texas seniors and to adults and children with disabilities. Applicants must live in Texas, be a U.S. citizen or qualified non-citizen, and be 65 or older or meet the Social Security definition of disability. Income is tested in dollars. From January 1, 2026 the SSI-based limit for community programs is $994 a month for one person ($1,491 for a couple); nursing facility, waiver and attendant care programs use a special limit of $2,982 ($5,964). The stored 224 percent of poverty is an estimate converting that highest limit for one person; community programs use the lower SSI-based limit. Resources must generally be $2,000 or less for one person ($3,000 for a couple). HHSC decides within 45 days, or 90 when disability must be established. The monthly value is an estimate of government spending per month for each aged or disabled enrollee, from the HHSC Reference Guide chart (year not labeled), not cash the household receives.
documents_needed: Proof of identity (driver's license or Texas DPS ID)
Immigration status papers (resident card I-551, I-94, or USCIS papers), if applicable
Social Security, SSI or pension award letter or pay stubs
Veterans benefits, workers' compensation or unemployment award letter or pay stubs
Legal representative papers (power of attorney, guardianship order, or court order), if applicable
Proof of Texas residence (utility bill, rent receipt, or landlord letter)

name: Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) Cash Help
description: TANF gives monthly cash payments to help Texas families with children pay for food, clothing, housing, utilities and other basics. It is for families with children age 18 or younger, either parents with their children or relatives caring for related children, who have little or no money. Eligibility depends on family income, the value of what the family owns or pays for, and child care and child support costs; accessible resources must be $1,000 or less. HHSC publishes dollar income limits and maximum grants by family size and household type; maximum monthly grants run from $130 to $545 for sizes 1 to 5. The stored 8 percent of poverty is an estimate from the $188 limit for a family of three with one caretaker, and the $338 monthly value is an estimate: the midpoint of the lowest and highest maximum grants, not an average grant. Parents must agree to work, child support, school and vaccine rules.
documents_needed: Proof of income (last two pay stubs or paychecks, employer statement, or self-employment records)
Bank account statements (most current for all accounts)
Proof a child is related to you (birth, hospital or baptismal certificate)
Proof of citizenship (U.S. passport, Certificate of Naturalization, U.S. birth certificate, hospital record of birth, or Medicare card)
Vaccine records for each child
Statement from a landlord or nonrelative neighbor that the child lives with you
Child support court papers or records, if anyone pays or gets child support
Copy of health insurance card or policy, if any

name: Unemployment Benefits
description: Texas unemployment benefits give temporary, partial income replacement to workers who lost their job or had their hours cut through no fault of their own. The program is paid for by employer taxes, not by workers. To qualify, a worker needs enough past wages earned in Texas and a qualifying job separation or hours reduction, must register for work search at WorkInTexas.com, and must be able, available and actively searching for work. People who are not U.S. citizens must be legally in the U.S. and authorized to work. The weekly benefit amount depends on past wages and currently ranges from $76 to $619; total benefits are capped at 26 times the weekly amount or 27 percent of base period wages, whichever is less. TWC says it takes about four weeks to learn whether you qualify. The monthly value shown is an estimate: the U.S. Department of Labor average weekly benefit for Texas times 52 divided by 12.
documents_needed: Social Security number
Valid state driver license or state ID card number
Last employer's business name, address and phone number
First and last dates worked for last employer
Hours worked and pay rate for the week you apply, if you worked
Information about the normal wage for the job you are seeking
DD Form 214 and service dates, if in the military in the past 18 months
Alien Registration number, if not a U.S. citizen or national

name: Medicaid for Parents and Caretakers
description: Texas Medicaid can cover a parent or other close relative who cares for a child that already has Medicaid. The child must live with you and be 17 or younger, or 18 and in school full time. Related caretakers include parents, step-parents, siblings, grandparents, aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews and first cousins. Income is tested in dollars, before taxes, by family size and by whether one or two parents are in the home, and the limits are very low: $230 a month for a one-parent family of three and $251 for a two-parent family of three. As a percent of the poverty level that is about 10% to 11%, so the percent shown is an estimate of the highest band. Coverage includes checkups, dental care, medicine, hospital care, X-rays, vision and hearing care, and specialists. The monthly value is an estimate of government spending per adult enrollee, not cash the household receives.
documents_needed: Proof of identity (current driver's license or Texas Department of Public Safety ID)
Immigration status papers (resident card I-551, I-94 or USCIS papers), if applicable
Proof of Texas residence (utility bill, rent receipt or letter from a landlord who is not a relative)
Proof of income and other benefits (award letters or pay stubs for Social Security, SSI, pension, veterans benefits, workers' compensation or unemployment)

name: Medicaid Buy-In for Adults (MBI)
description: Medicaid Buy-In gives low-cost Medicaid coverage to adults with disabilities who work. You must have a disability, work and live in Texas, and not live full time in a state institution or nursing home. People who already get Social Security disability benefits meet the disability rule, and others have their case reviewed. Income is tested in dollars: earnings from a job or self-employment must be under $3,325 a month before taxes, and countable assets can be no more than $5,000. That earnings limit is about 250% of the poverty level for one person, so the percent shown is an estimate. Some people pay a monthly fee of up to $500 based on their income. Coverage includes doctor visits, hospital care, medicine, vision and hearing care, mental health care and therapies.
documents_needed: Proof of identity (current driver's license or Texas Department of Public Safety ID)
Immigration status papers (resident card I-551, I-94 or USCIS papers), if applicable
Proof of Texas residence (utility bill, rent receipt or letter from a landlord who is not a relative)
Proof of income and other benefits (award letters or pay stubs for Social Security, SSI, pension, veterans benefits, workers' compensation or unemployment)

name: Primary Health Care Program
description: The Primary Health Care program gives low-cost checkups and basic medical care at clinics across Texas to people who cannot get the same care from another program. You qualify if you live in Texas, your income is at or below 200% of the federal poverty level, and you are not eligible for other programs or benefits that provide the same services. The program serves men, women and children. Services include diagnosis and treatment of common health problems, emergency services, family planning, immunizations and other preventive care, health education and counseling, and tests such as X-rays and lab work. You apply at a clinic site, and clinics can be found through 211 Texas. In certain cases services are available the same day you apply.

name: Vocational Rehabilitation Services
description: Vocational Rehabilitation helps Texans with disabilities prepare for, find, keep or advance in a job. You may qualify if you have a physical or mental condition that affects your ability to work, need these services to get or keep a job, and can get, keep or advance in a job after services. Eligibility does not depend on your income. People who get SSI or SSDI because of a disability are presumed eligible, and you must show you can legally work in the United States before you are found eligible. Services depend on your needs and can include counseling, training and job search help. A counselor decides eligibility within 60 days of your application, and a plan of services is written within 90 days after that.
documents_needed: Photo identification (driver's license, state-issued ID, school ID, passport or military ID) and your Social Security card, if you have them
Documentation showing you can legally work in the United States
Proof of income for you and your spouse, or your parents if they claim you as a dependent
Home and mailing address and the names and addresses of recent doctors, schools and employers
Names, addresses and phone numbers of two people who will always know how to contact you

name: Child Care Services (CCS) Scholarships
description: Child Care Services scholarships help Texas families pay for child care while parents work, look for work, or go to school or job training. A child must be under 13, or under 19 with a disability, and must be a U.S. citizen or have legal immigration status. Parents must need care to work or train for an average of at least 25 hours a week for a single parent, or 50 hours combined for two parents. Income is tested in dollars by family size: family income must be at or below 85% of the state median, for example $64,874 a year for a family of two, which is about 284% to 299% of the poverty level for families of two to six, so the percent shown is an estimate. Families pay a share of the cost of up to 7% of income.
documents_needed: Proof of the child's age, citizenship or immigration status and household (one document can cover all three)
Proof of family income, such as pay documents or an Employment/Income Verification Form
Information showing you need child care to work, look for work, or attend school or job training

name: Weatherization Assistance Program (WAP)
description: The Weatherization Assistance Program makes low-income homes cheaper to heat and cool by adding insulation, sealing air leaks and repairing or replacing inefficient heating and cooling equipment. Households qualify if their income is at or below 200% of the federal poverty guidelines, or if someone in the household received assistance payments under Title IV or XVI of the Social Security Act in the past 12 months. Local agencies run the program in all 254 Texas counties, and the state housing agency does not take applications from individuals, so you apply through a local provider. A home must be able to benefit from the work. The monthly value is an estimate based on the national average yearly energy savings reported by the Department of Energy, and the work itself is a one-time repair, not a monthly payment.
documents_needed: Proof of household income
Documentation showing who owns the home, collected by the local agency at the time of application
source: Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs

name: Senior Community Service Employment Program (SCSEP)
description: The Senior Community Service Employment Program gives part-time paid work and job training to older Texans with low incomes. You must be 55 or older, unemployed and able to work in the United States, and your family income can be no more than 125% of the federal poverty level. Participants work at nonprofit and public agencies such as schools, libraries and senior centers for an average of 20 hours a week, and are paid the highest of the federal, state or local minimum wage. The goal is to build skills and move into regular jobs. Priority goes to veterans and qualified spouses, then to people over 65, with a disability or at risk of homelessness, among others. The monthly value is an estimate of 20 hours a week at the federal minimum wage.

name: Senior Meals (Older Americans Act Nutrition Services)
description: Older Americans Act nutrition services provide meals to older Texans through local Area Agencies on Aging. Congregate meals, served in a group setting such as a senior center, are open to anyone 60 or older and to the spouse of a participant. Home-delivered meals are for people 60 or older who are frail and homebound or otherwise isolated and who score at least 20 on a needs evaluation. Spouses and, in some cases, people with disabilities who live with an eligible older person may also receive meals. The eligibility rules list no income test and there is no citizenship or residency requirement. Providers serve at least five meals a week. Call 800-252-9240 to reach your Area Agency on Aging.

name: Medicare Savings Programs (QMB, SLMB, QI-1)
description: Medicare Savings Programs help pay for all or some of your monthly Medicare payments, co-pays and deductibles. You must be entitled to Medicare Part A or Part B-ID. Income is tested in dollars by group: Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries have gross monthly income up to $1,330 for one person, Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiaries from $1,330.01 to $1,596, and the Qualifying Individuals program covers a person with income from $1,596 to less than $1,796 who is not otherwise getting Medicaid. Resource limits also apply. The top band is about 135% of the poverty level, so the percent shown is an estimate.

name: Texas Family Planning Program
description: The Texas Family Planning Program provides high-quality, comprehensive, low-cost and accessible family planning and reproductive health care services to eligible Texans. A man or woman is eligible if they are 64 years old or younger, live in Texas and have countable income that does not exceed 250% of the federal poverty level. Clinics must verify income, but they must waive that requirement when the verification would put the person's confidentiality at risk or be a barrier to receiving services. A person's eligibility must be assessed every year. Ask a participating clinic about fees, which depend on household income.

name: Texas Nurse-Family Partnership
description: The Texas Nurse-Family Partnership is a free, voluntary program where nurses partner with first-time mothers to improve prenatal care and provide one-on-one child development education and counseling. It serves first-time, low-income mothers and their families from the 28th week of pregnancy through the child's second birthday. To enroll you must have no previous live birth, have income at or below 185% of the federal poverty level, live in Texas and enroll before the end of the 28th week of pregnancy. In some special cases exceptions are made to the eligibility criteria. Providers serve selected communities, so ask where the program is offered near you.

name: Child Support Services (Texas Attorney General)
description: The Texas Attorney General's Child Support Division helps custodial parents with monitoring and enforcement of child support. Texas law requires a $35 annual service fee on cases that involve parents who have never received TANF. The fee is charged to custodial parents who receive full-service monitoring and enforcement and at least $550 in child support collections in a year, and it is deducted from the payment. It is not charged if TANF has ever been received in the case. The Legislature also authorized a $3 monthly State Disbursement Unit fee. There is no income test. The Attorney General's child support site explains how to get started.
source: Texas Office of the Attorney General

name: Texas Public School Prekindergarten
description: Texas public school prekindergarten serves eligible children in the year before kindergarten. A child must be four years of age on or before September 1 of the school year, or three if the district offers a three-year-old program, and must meet at least one condition. Two of them are being unable to speak and comprehend English and being educationally disadvantaged, which means eligible for the national school lunch program. Free lunch is available up to 130% and reduced-price lunch up to 185% of the federal poverty level, so the income shown is the highest band for that path. A district must offer prekindergarten if it identifies 15 or more eligible four-year-olds. Enroll through your local school district.

name: Independent Living Services
description: Independent Living Services help Texans with disabilities live in their own homes and communities for as long as possible. Core Services are free and are provided directly by a center for independent living, including information and referral, independent living skills training, peer counseling, advocacy and transition services. Purchased Services, such as hearing aids, home modifications, vehicle modifications, power wheelchairs and prosthetics, are provided on a sliding scale fee based on income, and evaluations that show which items would help most are provided at no cost. People with disabilities may have trouble with mobility, vision, hearing, communication, access to their home or vehicle, and daily activities.

name: Texas Benefits Counseling Program
description: The Texas Benefits Counseling Program aims to give all Texans aged 60 and older, and Medicare-eligible people with disabilities of any age, ready access to trained and certified benefits counselors. Regional benefits counselors, who are Area Agency on Aging employees, and volunteer counselors provide information, counseling, assistance and advocacy about benefits, entitlements and legal rights to people who are older, their families and caregivers who are Medicare-eligible. To reach your local Area Agency on Aging, call 800-252-9240. The page lists age and Medicare eligibility and no income test.

name: Texas Vaccines for Children
description: Texas Vaccines for Children makes it easier for children 0 to 18 years old to get vaccinated by offering low-cost vaccines to children who are uninsured, underinsured, covered by CHIP, of Native American or Native Alaskan heritage, or on Medicaid. The Texas Department of State Health Services runs the program and keeps a find-a-provider tool for families. Eligibility depends on the child's insurance status, not on household income, so a child with private insurance that covers vaccines is not in the program. Ask your child's doctor or clinic whether they are a Texas Vaccines for Children provider.
source: Texas Department of State Health Services
